name: Learn basic animal-track identification
blurb: Tracking turns a walk into a story. Start with the handful of species that live near you, and learn to read gait patterns as well as individual prints.
gear: A small ruler or a coin for scale
steps: Learn the big distinctions: cat prints show no claws and are round; dog and fox prints show claws and are oval; deer leave cloven slots; rodents show long-fingered hand-like prints.
Learn to measure — overall print length and width, and the stride between prints — and always photograph with something for scale.
Learn the four gait patterns: walkers, waddlers, bounders and gallopers. The pattern often identifies the family before the print does.
Learn the other signs: scat, browse lines, rubs, feathers, burrows and runs.
Visit the same muddy edge or riverbank weekly and log what you find.
Try trailing: follow one animal’s prints for 50 metres and work out what it was doing.
tips: Fresh clean prints in mud teach you far more than a dozen degraded ones in dust.
Domestic dogs confuse almost every beginner. Look for a straighter line of travel and no claw marks for cats.
proof: You identify five local species from prints alone and read a short trail as a sequence of behaviours.
